title: Only by deeds
hookLine: plants and animals differ by kind; humans differ only by what they do

cards: Two students, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, have been arguing on a walk. You may remember the name Vasettha from the Long Discourses.
One says a person is a brahmin, a member of the priestly class, by birth: pure lineage on both sides, seven generations back. The other says no, by conduct. Neither can convince the other.

So they do what friends still do when an argument stalls: they ask someone they both respect. The Buddha's answer, the ninth discourse of the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, starts not with people at all but with grass.

teach.h: GRASS AND BIRDS: MARKED BY BIRTH.
teach.b: Look at grasses and trees, the Buddha says. They don't claim anything, yet their kinds are marked by birth; you can tell one from another. Worms, moths, ants.
Four-footed animals, small and large. Snakes, fish, birds. Each kind has its own marks, given at birth.

Among people, he says, there are no such marks of birth: not in the hair, the head, the ears, the eyes, the mouth, the nose, the lips, the neck, the hands, the feet. Bodies differ, of course; he isn't denying that.
But nothing in the body marks out a separate kind. The differences people draw between each other are names they give.

teach.h: A FARMER IS ONE WHO FARMS.
teach.b: So what makes someone a farmer? Farming. A trader?
A priest? Performing the rites. And a true brahmin, in the noble sense the Buddha gives the word, is one who has let go, harms no one, is patient, honest, free.

teach.h: THE WORLD GOES ON BY ACTION.
teach.b: Then the line the whole answer leads to: the world goes on by action.
Beings are bound to their deeds, the poem says, as a moving chariot is held by its linchpin. You heard a cousin of this a few weeks back, in the outcast discourse: not by birth, by deeds.
Today adds the argument from nature. Grass is sorted by kind. People are known by what they do.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite the Vasettha Sutta when teaching that worth comes from conduct rather than birth.

o: a reward handed out by the gods
action, deed: what a person does
fate fixed at birth that can't change

games.q: only by deeds: tap the pairs.
p: how beings are bound to deeds

s: the Buddha says human bodies are all identical
he says there's no mark of a separate kind in the body, as there is between kinds of plants and animals.
in Sn 3.9 the world goes on by action
beings are bound to their deeds as a moving chariot is held by its linchpin.
the two students settled their argument before they met the Buddha
they couldn't convince each other, so they went to ask him.

games.q: two students ask whether a person is noble by birth or by conduct. where does the Buddha begin his answer?
o: with the family trees of well-known priests.
with grasses, trees, insects and animals.
games.why: he starts with nature: plants and animals have marks of kind from birth. people don't, so among people, deeds are what tell.

practice: Bring to mind someone you tend to file under a category: their accent, their job, their family, where they're from.
Set the label down for a moment and ask only what this person does: maybe they're patient with a child, maybe they show up early. Let the label go quiet, and let one deed stand there instead.

wordCard.voice: Kamma, deed or action. In the Vasettha Sutta, people aren't sorted by birth the way plants and animals are; they're known by what they do.

orig.note: Pali kamma (Sanskrit karma): action, deed. in Sn 3.9 the world goes on by kamma.

carryVoice: Your line: held by its linchpin. The wheel turns on what is done. That's day six hundred four.
